CASE STUDY 01

WhatsApp AI Customer Service + RAG

n8n export: Business Knowledge - Supabase RAG Ingestion
Business view

A customer messages a WhatsApp number with a question. The system waits briefly in case they send a few messages in a row (people often type in bursts), then reads all of them together, looks up the real answer in a private knowledge base of verified business facts, and replies — using only information that's actually true for that business, never a guess.

Technical view

An Evolution API webhook feeds inbound WhatsApp events into n8n. A Postgres function atomically buffers and batches messages per phone number. Once a batch is claimed, a LangChain AI Agent (Groq-backed) answers using a Supabase pgvector store exposed to it as a retrieval tool, and the reply is sent back through the Evolution API. A separate ingestion pipeline (Gemini embeddings + recursive text splitting) populates that vector store.

Business problem

Problem addressed: answering repetitive WhatsApp questions (hours, pricing, policies) manually doesn't scale, and a plain chatbot without a grounded knowledge source tends to invent answers.

Measured result: no measured business result is encoded in the workflow; this document focuses on the implemented automation architecture.

Trigger

An Evolution API Webhook (POST /evolution-whatsapp-inbound-v2) receives Evolution API's raw inbound-message payload for every WhatsApp event on the connected number — including messages the bot itself sends and group-chat traffic, which the workflow has to filter out itself. The initial payload includes the sender's WhatsApp JID, the message envelope (text, image caption, button/list reply, etc.), and event metadata.

End-to-end architecture
Evolution API Webhook │ ▼ Normalize & Validate (extract phone, message text, filter group/self/invalid events) │ ▼ Valid Private Message? ─── false ──▶ Ignore Invalid Event (stop) │ true ▼ Atomic Buffer + Batch Claim (Postgres fn: receive_whatsapp_message) │ ▼ Third Message – Process? ─── false ──▶ Stop – Waiting For More Messages │ true ▼ Get Claimed Three Messages (Postgres) │ ▼ Combine Customer Context │ ▼ AI Customer Service Agent ◀──tool──▶ Business Knowledge – Supabase RAG (pgvector) │ ▲ │ model: Groq Chat ▼ Prepare Reply – Preserve State (markdown → WhatsApp formatting) │ ▼ Send WhatsApp Reply – Evolution API │ ▼ Reset Batch After Successful Send (Postgres fn: reset_whatsapp_batch) ── separate ingestion pipeline ── Manual Trigger → Business Knowledge Input → Default Data Loader → Recursive Character Text Splitter → Gemini Embeddings → Insert into Supabase Vector Store
Step-by-step execution
Normalize & Validate — Code node
Input
Raw Evolution API webhook body.
Processing
Pulls the WhatsApp JID and strips it to a bare phone number; extracts the message text from whichever field Evolution API used (plain text, extended text, image/video caption, button reply, list reply); rejects the event if it was sent by the bot itself (fromMe), came from a group chat (JID ending @g.us), or isn't a message-type event.
Output
{ phone, messageId, messageText, instance, valid }
Why it matters
This is the validation layer — without it, group chatter and the bot's own replies would loop back into the AI agent.
Atomic Buffer + Batch Claim — Postgres node
Input
phone, messageId, messageText.
Processing
Calls a custom SQL function, receive_whatsapp_message(), defined in the workflow's own sticky-note documentation. It upserts a per-phone conversation row, appends the message (with duplicate protection via ON CONFLICT (external_message_id)), and only flags should_process = true once three messages have been buffered — a debounce pattern for people who send several WhatsApp messages in a row before pausing.
Output
{ batch_id, should_process, duplicate, message_count }
Why it matters
This is the difference between a toy webhook-to-AI wire-up and something that behaves correctly against how people actually use WhatsApp — it prevents the agent from replying three separate times to one thought split across three messages.
AI Customer Service Agent — LangChain Agent node (Groq)
Input
The combined customer_context string built from the batched messages.
Processing
A system prompt scopes the agent to a specific business, instructs it to call the business_knowledge_search tool for any factual claim, explicitly forbids inventing services, prices, hours or policies, tells it to admit when information isn't available rather than guess, forbids mentioning "RAG", "database" or internal tooling to the customer, and specifies WhatsApp-safe formatting (single-asterisk bold, single-underscore italics).
Output
A plain-text customer-facing reply.
Why it matters
The prompt design is doing real work here — grounding, tool-use discipline, and format constraints are all handled before a single character reaches the customer.
Business Knowledge – Supabase RAG — vectorStoreSupabase (retrieve-as-tool)
Input
A natural-language query generated by the agent when it decides it needs a fact.
Processing
Runs a similarity search against a Supabase pgvector documents table via a match_documents RPC call, returning the closest matching chunks of verified business knowledge.
Output
Retrieved text chunks, handed back to the agent as tool output.
Why it matters
This is the actual RAG mechanism — the model isn't answering from its own training data, it's answering from content the business owner controls.
Reset Batch After Successful Send — Postgres node
Input
phone, batch_id.
Processing
Calls reset_whatsapp_batch() to clear the buffered conversation state — but only after the WhatsApp reply has actually been sent.
Output
Confirmation row.
Why it matters
Ordering this after the send (not before) means a failed send doesn't silently wipe messages the customer still expects an answer to.
Data flow
WhatsApp message (Evolution API payload) → normalized {phone, text, instance} → buffered row in Postgres (conversation_messages) → 1–3 combined messages → customer_context string → AI Agent request (+ RAG tool calls as needed) → retrieved knowledge chunks (from documents table) → AI-generated reply text → WhatsApp-formatted reply (** → * conversion) → Evolution API send request → batch state reset
API integrations
ServiceWhy it's usedDirectionAuth
Evolution API (self-hosted WhatsApp gateway)Receive inbound WhatsApp messages; send repliesInbound webhook + outbound REST callAPI key header — [REDACTED] in this document
Supabase (Postgres + pgvector)Message buffering/state, vector knowledge storeRead/write via n8n Postgres & vector-store nodesSupabase credential (n8n-managed)
GroqLLM inference for the customer-service agentModel calls from the AI Agent nodeAPI credential (n8n-managed)
Google GeminiEmbeddings for the knowledge-ingestion pipelineOutbound embedding callsAPI credential (n8n-managed)

The live workflow calls the self-hosted Evolution API instance with a hardcoded API key and server address in the HTTP Request node. Both have been redacted from this document and should be rotated/rewritten as environment variables before the original JSON is shared with anyone.

WhatsApp integration

WhatsApp provider used in this workflow: Evolution API (a self-hosted WhatsApp gateway), for both inbound webhook handling and outbound message sending.

Other WhatsApp platforms I am comfortable working with: the official Meta WhatsApp Business/Cloud API, and I can adapt to whichever provider a project already uses.

Inbound handling covers text, extended text, image/video captions and button/list replies. Outbound handling sends plain text with WhatsApp-specific formatting (single-asterisk bold). There is no visible handling here for message delivery-status callbacks or media replies from the bot.

AI / LLM architecture

Provider / model: Groq-hosted chat model for the agent's reasoning; Google Gemini for embeddings on the ingestion side — two providers chosen for two different jobs (fast conversational inference vs. embedding quality).

Responsible for: interpreting the batched customer message, deciding when to call the knowledge-search tool, composing the natural-language reply, and formatting it for WhatsApp.

Not responsible for: message batching/debounce logic (handled by the Postgres function), knowledge retrieval mechanics (handled by the vector-store node's similarity search), or state management (handled by Code and Postgres nodes). The agent only decides what to say, using facts it is handed.

Database / storage

Supabase Postgres does two jobs here: a conversation_messages table plus a custom SQL function pair (receive_whatsapp_message, reset_whatsapp_batch) implement the atomic message-buffering state machine, and a separate documents table with a pgvector column stores embedded knowledge chunks, queried through a match_documents function for retrieval-augmented generation. Both the table DDL and the functions are included as SQL in the workflow's own sticky notes — this wasn't assembled purely from pre-built nodes; the underlying schema and batching logic were authored specifically for this use case.

Conditions and business logic
ConditionPurposeTrue pathFalse path
Valid Private Message?Filter out group chats, self-sent messages, invalid eventsContinue to bufferingIgnore Invalid Event (stop)
Third Message – Process?Debounce rapid-fire messages before replyingFetch batch & run the AI agentStop – Waiting For More Messages
Error handling and fallbacks

Reliability observations (present in the workflow): input validation before any processing; duplicate-message protection at the database level (ON CONFLICT); a debounce mechanism that avoids replying mid-thought; batch state is only cleared after a confirmed send.

Potential production considerations (recommendations, not existing features): retry/backoff on the outbound WhatsApp send if it fails; a dead-letter path for messages that never get a successful reply; monitoring/alerting on the Evolution API endpoint's health; moving the hardcoded API key and server address into n8n credentials/environment variables.

Security and data handling

The Postgres and Supabase connections use n8n-managed credentials rather than inline secrets. The Evolution API connection, by contrast, has an inline API key and server address in the node's parameters — flagged above for rotation. Credentials and the API key/server address have been removed and replaced with [REDACTED] throughout this document.

Testing

Recommended test cases:

  • Single message, three-in-a-row messages, and a message sent alone after a long pause
  • Group-chat message (should be dropped)
  • A message with no matching knowledge in the vector store (agent should say it doesn't know)
  • Duplicate webhook delivery of the same message ID
  • Evolution API send failure (batch should not reset)

CASE STUDY 02

ClinicFlow AI — WhatsApp Receptionist & Clinic Back Office

n8n export: ClinicFlow AI — Advanced Workflows (07–12 Combined) · 107 nodes
Business view

Patients message a Nigerian clinic's WhatsApp number — by typing or by voice note — and get a caring, bilingual (English/Pidgin) reply from an AI receptionist that can book an appointment, take payment, and knows to flag anything that sounds like a medical emergency. Around that core conversation, six background automations quietly handle reminders, win-back messages for patients who haven't returned, prescription refill nudges, post-visit check-ins, urgent lab-result alerts, and a patient referral rewards program.

Technical view

This is a combined export of one real-time conversational workflow plus six scheduled/event-triggered workflows sharing the same Supabase backend and Evolution API WhatsApp gateway. The core flow parses Evolution API payloads, transcribes voice notes with Gemini, looks up patient history in Supabase, runs a Groq-backed AI Agent with a structured JSON output contract, and routes on intent via a Switch node. Workflows 07–12 handle Paystack payments, reactivation, refills, follow-ups, lab-result escalation (with Termii SMS) and referrals.

Business problem

Problem addressed: a small clinic's front desk can't staff WhatsApp 24/7, misses patients who type in Pidgin or send voice notes, forgets to chase overdue reminders/refills/follow-ups, and has no way to react instantly when a lab result comes back urgent.

Measured result: no measured business result (e.g. reduced no-show rate, revenue recovered) is encoded in the workflow; this document focuses on the implemented automation architecture.

Trigger(s)

This export contains multiple independent triggers rather than one:

WorkflowTriggerStarts when…
Core receptionistWebhook (Evolution API)A WhatsApp message (text or voice) arrives
RemindersSchedule — every hourCron fires; checks for 24h/1h appointment windows
WF07 PaymentsWebhook (Paystack callback)Paystack confirms or updates a transaction
WF08 ReactivationSchedule — Monday 9AMWeekly win-back run
WF09 RefillsSchedule — daily 8AMDaily prescription check
WF10 Follow-upSchedule — daily 10AMDaily post-visit check
WF11 Lab resultsWebhook (staff-triggered)Clinic staff logs a lab result
WF12 ReferralsWebhook (appointment completed / code redeemed)An appointment is marked complete, or a new patient enters a referral code
End-to-end architecture — core receptionist flow
Webhook (Evolution API) ──▶ Acknowledge Webhook (instant 200 response) │ ▼ Parse Payload (sender, message type, text vs. voice, group filter) │ ▼ Skip Group Messages? ─── true ──▶ stop │ false ├──▶ Prepare Audio for Gemini ──▶ Transcribe a recording (Gemini 2.5 Flash, audio) │ ▼ (merge) Look Up Patient in Supabase + transcription branch ──▶ Merge │ ▼ Build Patient Context (new/returning, name, real message text) │ ▼ AI Agent (Groq + Simple Memory) — system prompt: clinic KB, emergency gate, no-diagnosis rule │ ▼ Parse AI Response (defensive JSON parse → intent / reply / action) │ ▼ Route by Action (Switch) ├── general reply ──────────▶ Send WhatsApp Reply ├── emergency ─────────────▶ Send Emergency Reply + Log Emergency to Supabase └── booking ───────────────▶ Get Available Doctors → Find Doctor & Available Slots → No Doctor Available? ─true─▶ Send No Doctor Message ─false▶ Save Pending Booking → Send Slot Options │ ▼ Log Message to Supabase
Step-by-step execution — core flow
Parse Payload — Code node
Input
Raw Evolution API webhook body.
Processing
Extracts sender phone/name from the WhatsApp JID, flags group messages for skipping, and determines whether the incoming message is text or a voice note — setting a [VOICE_NOTE_PENDING_TRANSCRIPTION] placeholder for voice notes until the Gemini transcription step fills it in.
Output
{ senderPhone, senderName, patientMessage, isVoiceNote, skip }
Why it matters
This single node absorbs all the messiness of a real WhatsApp payload before anything downstream has to think about it.
Transcribe a recording — Google Gemini node (audio resource, gemini-2.5-flash)
Input
The binary audio attachment for voice-note messages.
Processing
Sends the audio to Gemini for transcription.
Output
Transcribed text, later substituted in for the placeholder in Build Patient Context.
Why it matters
Voice notes are a very common way Nigerian WhatsApp users communicate — this makes the receptionist accessible to people who'd rather speak than type.
Build Patient Context — Code node
Input
Merged output of the parse/transcription branch and the Supabase patient lookup.
Processing
Determines new vs. returning patient from whether a Supabase record exists, resolves the real message text (transcription if it was a voice note), and assembles a single structured context string for the AI Agent.
Output
A context object/string the agent's prompt is built from.
Why it matters
Keeps patient-identity logic out of the prompt itself and in testable, deterministic code.
AI Agent — LangChain Agent (Groq Chat Model + Simple Memory buffer window)
Input
Patient context (phone, name, message, new/returning status, timestamp).
Processing
A detailed system prompt defines the assistant as "ClinicFlow AI", specifies it speaks formal English and Nigerian Pidgin, embeds a small clinic knowledge base directly (hours, named doctors, consultation fees, location), and lays out priority rules evaluated in order — an emergency gate checked first, then an explicit "you are a receptionist, NOT a doctor — no diagnosis" guardrail, then normal conversation/booking handling. It is instructed to return structured JSON.
Output
JSON: { intent, reply, action }
Why it matters
Putting patient safety rules ahead of everything else in the prompt, and constraining the model to structured output the rest of the workflow can branch on, is the difference between a chatbot and a receptionist system.
Parse AI Response — Code node
Input
Raw agent output.
Processing
Strips markdown code fences the model sometimes adds, attempts JSON.parse, and falls back to a safe generic reply (intent: GENERAL) inside a try/catch if parsing fails, rather than crashing the execution.
Output
{ intent, replyMessage, action, ...patient context }
Why it matters
LLM output is not guaranteed to be valid JSON — this node is the safety net that keeps a malformed response from breaking the whole conversation.
Find Doctor & Available Slots — Code node
Input
Requested doctor name (if any) and the list of doctors from Supabase, plus already-booked appointment times.
Processing
Matches the requested doctor (or defaults to the first available), builds a list of open time slots, and explicitly excludes hours that are already booked by comparing against real scheduled appointments (not just a static availability calendar).
Output
Selected doctor + a list of genuinely open slots, or a "no doctor available" flag.
Why it matters
This is real scheduling logic, not a placeholder — it reconciles two live data sources before offering a slot.
Supporting automations (WF07–WF12)

WF07 — Paystack Payment: after a slot is chosen, WF07 | Initialize Paystack creates a Paystack transaction (amount, reference, metadata linking it back to the booking) and a payment link is sent over WhatsApp; the booking status moves to "Awaiting Payment". A second webhook, WF07 | Paystack Confirms Payment, receives Paystack's callback, filters out non-payment events, verifies success, creates the confirmed appointment, closes the pending-booking record, and notifies both the patient and clinic staff.

WF08 — Reactivation Engine: every Monday at 9AM, patients are bucketed by days since their last visit (30/60/90) and sent a tiered WhatsApp win-back message per bucket.

WF09 — Prescription Refill: daily at 8AM, active prescriptions are pulled from Supabase and filtered to those due for a refill reminder, then marked as reminded. This export doesn't show a distinct outbound WhatsApp-send node in the WF09 branch the way the other reminder flows do — it may share a send node upstream, or this branch may be incomplete in this export. Flagging rather than assuming.

WF10 — Post-Visit Follow-Up: daily at 10AM, appointments completed roughly three days earlier are pulled, a check-in message is built and sent, and the follow-up is logged.

WF11 — Lab Results Notification: a staff-triggered webhook parses a lab result, saves it, and notifies the patient by WhatsApp. If the result is flagged urgent, it additionally sends an SMS alert to clinic staff via Termii and creates a dashboard alert record — a dual-channel escalation path for anything time-sensitive.

WF12 — Referral Reward System: on appointment completion, a referral code is generated (guarded by a "first time?" check so a returning patient doesn't get issued duplicate codes). A second webhook path handles a new patient redeeming someone else's code: it looks up the referrer, calculates a fixed-amount reward, updates the referrer's credit balance, and sends confirmation messages to both parties.

Data flow
WhatsApp message (text or voice) → parsed sender + message (+ Gemini transcription if voice) → merged with Supabase patient record → structured patient context → AI Agent request → structured JSON {intent, reply, action} → routed by action: general → WhatsApp reply emergency→ WhatsApp reply + Supabase emergency log booking → doctor/slot lookup → pending booking → Paystack payment → confirmed appointment → confirmation + reminders → conversation logged to Supabase

WhatsApp integration

WhatsApp provider used in this workflow: Evolution API — same self-hosted pattern as Workflow 01, reused consistently across both.

Other WhatsApp platforms I am comfortable working with: the official Meta WhatsApp Business/Cloud API and other providers, as required by a project.

Inbound handling covers both text and voice notes (with transcription), and filters out group messages. Outbound handling covers replies, slot options, payment links, reminders, and emergency messages — all as plain text with WhatsApp-safe formatting.

AI / LLM architecture

Providers / models: Groq for the receptionist's conversational reasoning (with an n8n Simple Memory buffer window for short-term conversational context), and Gemini 2.5 Flash specifically for audio transcription — two different models used for two different, well-matched jobs.

Responsible for: understanding the patient's message, detecting emergencies, holding a bilingual conversational tone, and deciding intent/action.

Not responsible for: actual scheduling arithmetic (handled deterministically in Find Doctor & Available Slots), payment processing (handled by the Paystack integration), or referral reward calculation (handled in dedicated Code nodes). The model decides intent and tone; code decides facts and numbers.

Database / storage

Supabase is the system of record across the whole clinic system: patients, conversation logs, doctor availability, appointments/bookings (pending and confirmed), prescriptions, referral codes and credit balances, and dashboard alerts for urgent lab results. Each of the six supporting workflows reads and writes to this same backend, which is what lets a single patient's history stay consistent across the receptionist conversation, reminders, reactivation, and referrals.

Error handling and fallbacks

Reliability observations (present in the workflow): the webhook acknowledges immediately before heavy processing runs; group and self-sent messages are filtered early; the AI's JSON output is parsed defensively with a safe fallback reply on parse failure; slot availability is checked against real bookings rather than assumed; Paystack webhook events are filtered to only process actual payment confirmations.

Potential production considerations (recommendations, not existing features): no dedicated error-trigger workflow was found in this export (unlike Workflow 03's dedicated Error Trigger); I'd add one, plus retry logic on the Evolution API and Termii sends, monitoring on the Paystack webhook path specifically (payment confirmations failing silently is a real business risk), and moving all inline API keys into n8n credentials.

Security and data handling

Patient data (name, phone, message content, health-adjacent context) flows through Supabase and the AI Agent — this is sensitive data by nature, which is exactly why the prompt's "no diagnosis" and emergency-first rules matter as much as the plumbing. Credentials and the Evolution API / Paystack / Termii keys that were hardcoded in this export have been redacted from this document.

Testing

Recommended test cases:

  • Text message vs. voice-note message, including a voice note the transcription step fails on
  • A message containing emergency-flagged language
  • Booking a slot that's already taken between the offer and the confirmation
  • Paystack webhook firing for an unrelated event type
  • A lab-result submission marked urgent vs. routine
  • A referral code redeemed twice by the same new patient

CASE STUDY 03

StockGuard — Shopify Inventory Intelligence

n8n export: StockGuard — Shopify Inventory Intelligence
Business view

Every time a Shopify store's stock level changes, this system checks whether that product is now low, critical, or sold out — using rules the merchant sets, not guesswork — logs the event, updates the product's status, and emails an alert if action is needed. Once a day, it also emails the merchant a plain-language summary of the store's overall inventory health.

Technical view

A Shopify inventory webhook (HMAC-verified) feeds a validation and deduplication pipeline, then a deterministic Code node computes stock status, days-of-runway, risk score and reorder recommendations against product data stored in Airtable, and writes the results back. Alerts, stockout/restock/anomaly events are logged as Airtable records and emailed via Gmail. A separate daily-scheduled branch aggregates the day's data and uses a Gemini-backed AI Agent — restricted to summarizing pre-calculated facts — to write a digest email.

Business problem

Problem addressed: merchants find out about stockouts and slow-moving anomalies after the fact, from a spreadsheet nobody checks daily, rather than the moment stock actually changes.

Measured result: no measured business result (e.g. stockouts avoided, revenue protected) is encoded in the workflow; this document focuses on the implemented automation architecture.

Trigger

Two independent triggers in one workflow:

  • Shopify Inventory Webhook — POST /stockguard-inventory, fired by Shopify on every inventory-level change, with raw body capture enabled so the HMAC signature can be verified against the exact bytes Shopify sent.
  • Daily 8AM Trigger — a schedule trigger that kicks off the daily digest branch.

The initial webhook payload includes inventory_item_id, location_id, and the new available quantity.

End-to-end architecture
-- Real-time path -- Shopify Inventory Webhook │ ▼ Verify & Normalize (HMAC check, field validation, idempotency key) │ ▼ IF Valid ─false─▶ Log Rejected │ true ▼ Check Duplicate (Airtable Events) ──▶ IF Is New ─false─▶ Log Duplicate │ true ▼ Get Product (Airtable Products) ──▶ Intelligence (deterministic rules engine) │ ▼ IF Product Found ─false─▶ Log Unmapped │ true ▼ Create Event + Update Product (Airtable) │ ├──▶ IF Send Alert ──▶ Record Alert + email merchant ├──▶ IF Stockout ──▶ Create Stockout record ├──▶ IF Restock ──▶ Find Open Stockout → Prepare Close → Close Stockout └──▶ IF Anomaly ──▶ Create Anomaly record │ ▼ Log Success Error Trigger (dedicated) ──▶ Config (Errors) ──▶ Log Error (Airtable) -- Daily digest path -- Daily 8AM Trigger ──▶ Get All Products + Get Recent Events (24h) ──▶ Build Report Facts (deterministic) ──▶ AI Summary (Gemini agent, facts-only) ──▶ Record Report (Airtable) ──▶ Send digest email (Gmail)
Step-by-step execution
Verify & Normalize — Code node
Input
Raw webhook headers + body (rawBody captured for signing).
Processing
If a SHOPIFY_WEBHOOK_SECRET environment variable is configured, computes an HMAC-SHA256 digest of the raw request body and compares it to Shopify's x-shopify-hmac-sha256 header using a timing-safe comparison; validates that inventory_item_id, location_id and a numeric available value are present; builds an idempotency-style event key.
Output
{ valid, errors[], event, hmacStatus }
Why it matters
This is genuine webhook-security practice — timing-safe HMAC verification, not just "trust whatever hits the endpoint".
Intelligence — Code node
Input
The validated event plus the matched Airtable product record.
Processing
Explicitly commented in the code as deterministic — "the AI is NOT involved here". Computes stock status (HEALTHY / LOW_STOCK / CRITICAL / SOLD_OUT) against the product's low-stock threshold and a critical ratio, estimates days-of-runway from average daily sales, calculates a risk score, decides whether a reorder is needed, and detects stockout, restock, and anomaly transitions (e.g. an unusually large drop or rise versus expected sales velocity) against merchant-configurable thresholds (anomalyDropPct, anomalyRisePct, cooldownMinutes, etc. — all set in the Config (Ingest) node).
Output
A structured object of computed fields for the Event, Product update, and (conditionally) Alert / Stockout / Anomaly records.
Why it matters
This is the core intellectual property of the workflow — a rules engine, not a single IF statement, and it's kept deliberately separate from the AI layer used elsewhere in the workflow.
Prepare Close Stockout — Code node
Input
The open Stockout record and the restock event.
Processing
Computes the stockout's duration in hours from its recorded start time to the restock timestamp.
Output
{ recordId, fields: { Status: 'CLOSED', Duration Hours, ... } }
Why it matters
Turns a raw restock event into an actual operational metric (how long was this product actually out of stock) rather than just flipping a status flag.
Build Report Facts — Code node
Input
All products and the last 24 hours of events, fetched from Airtable.
Processing
Again explicitly commented as deterministic — "AI only summarizes these". Counts products by status, ranks the top-5 highest-risk products, lists products needing reorder, lists open stockouts, and lists the day's restocks and anomalies.
Output
A structured facts JSON object.
Why it matters
Same architectural discipline as Intelligence — the numbers are computed in code before the AI ever sees them.
AI Summary — LangChain Agent (Google Gemini)
Input
The facts JSON from Build Report Facts.
Processing
System prompt instructs the model to write a maximum-150-word summary using only the numbers and names in the JSON, never invent or estimate quantities, never override a calculated status or risk score, and — notably — never claim fraud, theft or a sync failure for an anomaly, instead saying "manual review recommended".
Output
Plain-language digest text.
Why it matters
This is a deliberate guardrail against a real failure mode of AI-written business reports: a model speculating about causes (like theft) that the data can't actually support.
Data flow
Shopify inventory webhook (item, location, available qty) → HMAC-verified + validated event → matched Airtable product record → computed stock status / risk / runway / reorder flag → Airtable Event + updated Product record → conditional Alert / Stockout / Anomaly records + merchant email (daily) All products + 24h events → deterministic report facts → AI-written plain-language summary → Airtable Report record + digest email
API integrations
ServiceWhy it's usedDirectionAuth
ShopifySource of inventory-change eventsInbound webhookHMAC-SHA256 signature verification
AirtableOperational database — Products, Events, Alerts, Stockouts, Anomalies, Reports, LogsRead/write via RESTAirtable Personal Access Token (predefined credential type)
Google GeminiWriting the daily-digest summary from pre-computed factsOutboundAPI credential (n8n-managed)
GmailSending alert and daily-digest emailsOutboundOAuth credential (n8n-managed)

Airtable is accessed directly via authenticated HTTP requests to its REST API rather than through n8n's native Airtable node — every Create/Update/Query operation is a hand-built request with its own filterByFormula logic.

AI / LLM architecture

Provider / model: Google Gemini, used in a single, narrow role.

Responsible for: turning a JSON object of already-calculated facts into a short, readable summary for a human merchant.

Not responsible for: anything numerical or decisional. Stock status, risk scoring, reorder thresholds, stockout/restock/anomaly detection, and the daily facts themselves are all computed in plain JavaScript before the model is ever called. This is the clearest example across all four workflows of separating deterministic business logic from AI narration — a distinction that matters a lot for a system merchants have to trust with their inventory numbers.

Database / storage

Airtable serves as the full operational datastore: Products (current/previous stock, thresholds, computed status and risk), Events (every inventory change, used for both audit and duplicate detection), Alerts, Stockouts (opened and closed), Anomalies, Logs (errors and rejections) and Reports (daily digest history). Every table is queried and written through direct Airtable REST calls with formula-based filtering (e.g. matching a product by Inventory Item ID, or finding events in the last 24 hours).

Conditions and business logic
ConditionPurposeTrue pathFalse path
IF ValidReject malformed/unverified webhook payloadsContinueLog Rejected
IF Is NewDeduplicate webhook redeliveryContinueLog Duplicate
IF Product FoundHandle inventory items not mapped in AirtableContinueLog Unmapped
IF Send Alert / Stockout / Restock / AnomalyRoute to the relevant Airtable record + notificationCreate record (+email where relevant)Skip that branch
Error handling and fallbacks

Reliability observations (present in the workflow): HMAC signature verification with a timing-safe comparison; explicit field validation with itemized error messages; duplicate-event protection via an idempotency key; a dedicated Error Trigger node that catches failures anywhere in the workflow and logs them to Airtable separately from the happy path, including the failing node name and execution ID.

Potential production considerations (recommendations, not existing features): retry/backoff on the Airtable HTTP calls (Airtable rate-limits at a fixed request/second cap, which a burst of Shopify webhooks could hit); alerting (e.g. Slack/PagerDuty) on top of the existing Airtable error log, rather than requiring someone to check the Logs table; execution-history retention policy for the Shopify webhook workflow given its expected volume.

Security and data handling

Shopify webhook authenticity is verified cryptographically rather than assumed. Airtable access uses a scoped personal access token via n8n's predefined credential type rather than an inline key. The Airtable base identifier referenced throughout the workflow has been generalized to {BASE_ID} in this document, and the merchant's personal email address that appeared in one node has been redacted.

Testing

Recommended test cases (plus what the screenshots already show was run):

  • Valid webhook with a correct HMAC signature, and one with a tampered/missing signature
  • A stock change for a product not yet mapped in Airtable
  • Duplicate delivery of the same Shopify webhook event
  • A drop large enough to trigger the anomaly threshold
  • Restocking a product that has an open stockout record
  • Daily digest run with zero events in the last 24 hours

The included execution-log screenshot shows this workflow was actually run repeatedly against real or realistic data (multiple successful executions between 924ms and 8.9s), not only designed.

Why this workflow is relevant to an AI automation agency: it's the strongest example of correct AI/automation architecture in this portfolio — a rules engine handles the numbers, an AI model only narrates them — plus it's the one workflow here with independently verifiable proof across three separate systems (Shopify's own webhook config, Airtable's live data, and n8n's execution history).
CASE STUDY 04

GHL Document-to-PDF — Contact Agreement Generator

n8n export: GHL Document to PDF - Contact Agreement Generator
Business view

When a GoHighLevel workflow needs to hand a customer a signed-looking agreement — with their name, address, payment plan and package details already filled in — this automation builds that document automatically, converts it to a real PDF, and attaches it straight back to the customer's record. No one has to manually fill in a template.

Technical view

A webhook receives a GHL workflow action's payload, fetches the full contact record from the GoHighLevel API, string-templates a branded HTML document with the contact's custom-field data, sends that HTML to PDFShift for conversion to a PDF binary, and uploads the resulting file back to the contact's custom field via GoHighLevel's multipart upload endpoint — with explicit success/error branches and JSON responses at each stage.

Business problem

Problem addressed: manually generating and attaching a populated agreement PDF for every customer inside a CRM is repetitive and error-prone.

Measured result: no measured business result is encoded in the workflow; this document focuses on the implemented automation architecture.

Trigger

Webhook - GHL Workflow Trigger — POST /ghl-agreement-pdf, called by a GoHighLevel workflow action. The initial payload includes the contact ID, location ID, and a set of custom-field values (spouse/co-customer name, payment schedule, agreement ID, service date, package summary, amount paid, remaining balance, and contact details like name/email/phone/address).

End-to-end architecture
Webhook - GHL Workflow Trigger │ ▼ Extract Contact + Location IDs │ ▼ GHL - Get Contact ──▶ IF Contact Found ─false─▶ Error - Contact Not Found ─▶ Log Error ─▶ Respond - Error │ true ▼ Build Populated HTML (string-templated agreement document) │ ▼ PDFShift - Convert HTML to PDF ──▶ IF PDF Generated ─false─▶ Error - PDF Generation Failed ─▶ Log Error ─▶ Respond - Error │ true ▼ GHL - Upload PDF to Custom Field (multipart upload) │ ▼ Log Success ──▶ Respond - Success
Step-by-step execution
Extract Contact + Location IDs — Code node
Input
The raw GHL webhook body.
Processing
Pulls the contact ID and location ID (falling back between two possible payload shapes), plus name/email/phone/address and every agreement-specific custom field (spouse name, payment schedule, agreement ID, service date, package summary, amount paid, remaining balance).
Output
A flat object of every field the document template needs.
Why it matters
Isolates GHL's payload quirks into one node so the rest of the workflow works with clean, predictable field names.
Build Populated HTML — Code node
Input
The extracted contact/agreement fields.
Processing
Renders a complete, styled HTML document (a branded header/logo layout and structured content sections) by templating the real values into an HTML string, entirely in code rather than an external templating service.
Output
{ populatedHtml, fileName, contactId, locationId }
Why it matters
Shows comfort building a real HTML document generator by hand, not just filling placeholders in a pre-made template file.
PDFShift - Convert HTML to PDF — HTTP Request node
Input
The populated HTML string.
Processing
POSTs to PDFShift's /v3/convert/pdf endpoint with the HTML as the source, requesting a binary/file response.
Output
A PDF binary attached to the item.
Why it matters
Cleanly separates "build the document" from "render it to PDF" — a reusable pattern for any GHL/CRM document-generation need.
GHL - Upload PDF to Custom Field — HTTP Request node
Input
The PDF binary and the contact/location IDs.
Processing
POSTs a multipart/form-data request to GoHighLevel's custom-fields upload endpoint, attaching the PDF as binary form data against the contact's ID.
Output
GHL's upload confirmation response.
Why it matters
Closes the loop — the generated document ends up exactly where staff would look for it, inside the contact's own CRM record.
Data flow
GHL workflow webhook payload → extracted contact/agreement fields → verified against a live GHL contact lookup → populated HTML document (string) → PDF binary (via PDFShift) → uploaded to the contact's custom field in GHL → JSON success/error response back to the calling GHL workflow
API integrations
ServiceWhy it's usedDirectionAuth
GoHighLevel API (v2021-07-28)Fetch contact data; upload the finished PDF to a custom fieldOutbound REST, both directionsHeader auth (n8n generic credential)
PDFShiftConvert the generated HTML into a real PDFOutboundHeader auth (n8n generic credential)

Both integrations use n8n's generic header-auth credential type rather than inline keys — nothing to redact here.

Database / storage

No dedicated database — GoHighLevel itself is the system of record; the contact's custom field is the storage location for the generated document. This keeps the workflow stateless and simple by design.

Conditions and business logic
ConditionPurposeTrue pathFalse path
IF Contact FoundStop early if the contact ID from the webhook doesn't resolveContinue to document buildError - Contact Not Found
IF PDF GeneratedConfirm PDFShift actually returned binary data before attempting uploadContinue to GHL uploadError - PDF Generation Failed
Error handling and fallbacks

Reliability observations (present in the workflow): both external calls (GHL lookup, PDFShift conversion) are followed by an explicit success check before proceeding; every failure path routes through one shared Log Error node with a labeled errorStage and errorDetail, and returns a structured JSON error response rather than letting the webhook caller get an opaque failure; the code comments explicitly note this is designed as "ONE place to add real alerting later (Slack/email) without touching the rest of the workflow".

Potential production considerations (recommendations, not existing features): the alerting the code comments anticipate isn't implemented yet — currently errors only reach console.error and the webhook response; retry logic on the PDFShift call for transient failures; the PDFShift request currently uses "sandbox": true, which should be switched off for real production documents.

Security and data handling

Both external APIs are called through n8n's generic header-auth credential type, keeping keys out of the workflow JSON itself. A test contact's personal email address that appeared in this export's pinned example data has been redacted from this document.

Testing

Recommended test cases:

  • A valid contact ID with all custom fields populated
  • An invalid or deleted contact ID
  • Missing/blank custom fields (e.g. no spouse name)
  • PDFShift returning an error instead of a binary (e.g. malformed HTML)
  • GHL upload failing after a successful PDF conversion
